This study investigates the utility of pretrained models in continual learning (CL) specifically for sentence classification. We established a robust benchmark using a simplified setup: ten binary tasks built from single classification data sources. Utilizing a regression-based approach, we created a strong baseline by training an identical multi-task CL model across all tasks without any pretrained weights or additional architectural features. Our results indicate that the proposed method achieves performance near the state-of-the-art on each individual task, yielding less than a 0.5 standard deviation gap compared to top benchmarks while incurring minimal data usage per task—requiring only approximately 10% of the training instances per task relative to the frequency of common protocols. The uniqueness and efficacy of this robust baseline are explicitly detailed to facilitate more meaningful future evaluations in CL research.

The surge in processing capacity and the availability of massive datasets have enabled significant advancements in computational physics, chemistry, and engineering, largely driven by Algorithm22 models. These systems rely on large-scale training to achieve peak performance, necessitating constant updates as new data becomes accessible to remain effective. To enable continuous skill enhancement through ongoing learning, we review the Instructor-Student architecture. In this framework, instructors are initially trained on historical datasets to acquire relevant patterns. Subsequently, student networks are fine-tuned by the integrated knowledge of these instructors, resulting in outputs that align closely with those of the trained instructors. This approach reduces the time and cost associated with training on new information, eliminating the need for retraining on extensive streams of data. While this survey offers a comprehensive overview of the theory behind these architectures, it also identifies promising directions for upcoming research.

This work investigates the transition in randomly packed microsphere systems, characterized by an abrupt rise in viscosity and transition from flowing to arrested non-Newtonian behavior as shear rate increases. This paper addresses robust input-constrained control barrier function (ICCBF) synthesis for secure controller design against constant disturbances. Input-constrained control barrier functions serve as a method to guarantee safety properties under bounded disturbances while respecting arbitrary affine input limits; these affine constraints commonly appear in networked control systems due to communication limitations and in physical systems due to hardware restrictions. The main difficulty in solving ICCBF problems with unrestricted input matrices represents only a minor hurdle, often resolving easily as a quadratic program (QP), becomes computationally demanding and nonconvex when inputs are subject to various affine constraints. To overcome this difficulty, we adopt a strategy that transforms the original ICCBF determination into a set of underlying model predictive controllers (MPC), effectively reconfiguring the problem constraints into modified state input restrictions with significantly simpler structure. We analyze key attributes of the resulting equivalent formulation, demonstrating that solutions found via these constraints produce a mapping equivalent to that derived from ICCBFs, thus preserving system safety. We then apply this approach to the control synthesis of several nonlinlinear dynamic systems, showing how the technique can be integrated with sampling-based planners like rapid randomized tree (RRT*) to determine both discrete and continuous controls in environments with hurdles and dead zones while maintaining security guarantees.

Regionalism has become a significant focus within the research on representable mathematical regions, traditionally analyzed through the lens of topology and order theory. This work represents the confluence of a topological and a representable approach, beginning with the introduction of a novel definition for representable regions that relies on approximation spaces. Specifically, this framework assigns to each set of open sets the property of containing region(s) if, and only if, their intersection forms a region; the authors demonstrate that this induced relationship satisfies all requisite representations of regionality. They subsequently examine the connection between this new topology-based definition and earlier, existing definitions of representability. A key contribution involves the introduction of a specific system of open sets termed "connectivity-harmonic sets," established to define regionality through a more restrictive representation. The authors conclude by presenting several innovative definitions of regionality that integrate both topology and representability, while also defining new forms of "quasi-representable regions" and determining the topological closure of the set of regionals.

This study examines the direction-dependent resistance to dragging a cylinder within dry, liquid-saturated granular beds. We demonstrate experimentally that as saturation increases, the contrast between lateral and vertical friction becomes more pronounced. Additionally, we identify a transition to negative slip flow between the object's axis height $H$ and the free surface level, which amplifies the overall shape dependence of the drag force, as opposed to downward motion. These findings are reconciled within an effective viscosity model, which accurately predicts shape-dependent drag forces across varying degrees of fluid saturation in granular media. This study emphasizes how findings highlight the shape-dependent nature of the drag force, predicted by an effective viscosity model, which is particularly useful when understanding movement dynamics of cylindrical objects in fluid-saturated granular systems at the microscopic scale. We also explore how finding a strong agreement with experimental measurements, we can understand better the role played by capillary forces and particle rearrangements on the motion of cylinders in these complex environments. By the end, this work provides new theoretical insights and highlights the importance considering both fluid content and particle arrangement to explain the observed anisotropy effects.

Achieving the pinnacle of performance in computing system design and configuration is vital for maximizing system yield. Bayesian Optimization (BO) has emerged as a preferred strategy for this goal, especially in environments involving numerous variables where experimental data (logs, traces, or traces) abounds. However, exploring the parameter space efficiently remains challenging when each experimental run incurs substantial time, as full logs retrieval further slows down the process. We introduced Graphical Bayesian Optimization (BoGraph), a technique that leverages the structural links within expansive, organized logs—establishing a Bayesian network to encode dependencies among variables. By conducting incremental inference over BoGraph, we accomplish a simultaneous update using every observation across all points in the parameter space, and can quickly propose new experiments via direct Bayesian sampling. Our experiments, conducted on real and mock systems featuring millions of observations and evaluating up to a 10,000 times faster speed improvements for novelty proposals compared to standard BO.

In response to the rising tendency for applications to migrate from cloud environments to edge nodes, there is a critical need for an event-driven evaluation (EDE) framework capable of processing streaming data at the edge. This framework must uphold robustness and transparency against various forms of Skewness in underlying event-ordering, particularly since current database technologies—both event stores and stream processing engines—are only partially able to guarantee strict monotonicity or consistency. Furthermore, traditional approaches require substantial retooling to incorporate EDE. Our framework introduces a universal, user-friendly interface for expressing such drives. Key features of this approach include a framework-independent, application-specific distribution of functions across edge nodes, as well as efficient, transparent mitigation of Skewness. We have validated our framework through a resilience test involving the Netflix Outage of 2021 and real-world benchmarks, demonstrating that EDE ensures consistency and performance while requiring minimal application-specific adjustments.

The ATLAS collaboration at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) possesses significant capabilities for the precise study of rare and CP-violating decays in B mesons, leveraging high statistics, excellent flavor tagging, momentum resolution, and efficient rejection of background noise. This paper presents findings on the study of B_meson mixing and CP violation, including the analysis of the rare decay channel.

Our approach focuses on the challenge of synthesizing plausible traffic scenarios, a task crucial for the development and evaluation of autonomous driving systems. We introduce a deep neural network framework optimized with a specialized traffic loss function, enabling the mapping of random latent vectors into traffic scenerios rich in realism and diverse traffic participant behavior. Parsed traffic elements—including 3D bounding boxes, velocity data, and centric ID assignments for both vehicles and pedestrians—are generated from these latent vectors via a shared, multi-task learning architecture. This poses the complex problem of aligning these multi-dimensional parts onto a two-dimensional image while adhering strictly to their physical and logical prior constraints, which we address to ensure generation success. These priors encompass spatial constraints, temporal consistency, common-sense traffic protocols, and ethical considerations. These factors have been incorporated into our unique traffic loss function, which serves as a differentiable differentiator, facilitating end-to-end backpropagation through the generator along with the encoding decoding components processing random latent inputs. This derivative setup allows the network to directly learn from loss minimization. To confirm our model's robustness and versatility, we conducted extensive experiments across an expansive and varied dataset. The results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

We examine the Ising model within a Cayley tree context, demonstrating the existence of new weakly periodic Gibbs states. By identifying conditions under which such states exist, we identify them as arises when either $|\tan(2\omega)\sin\lambda| < 1$ or when $\omega$ and $\lambda$ satisfy specific related constraints; these states are characterized parametrically by a pair of real numbers, $\omega$ and $\lambda$.

Developing numerical schemes for time-dependent partial differential equations often entails two main goals: maintaining desirable properties like positivity or conservation laws while achieving rapid solution speeds. This paper introduces a versatile application of Preconditioned Krylov methods suitable for modern Higham-Gemignani structure-preserving discretizations, which typically yield non-trivial, intricate matrix structures. We provide detailed analysis of the underlying algorithms, proving that this approach preserves the inherent mathematical features of the matrices associated with both the time-stepping and spatial discretization processes. Specifically, we illustrate the implementation and performance of this method on the conservation laws for Euler and Maxwell equations, along with a general application framework, and present visualizations of the convergence behavior within the resulting preconditioned system.

Matching a surgical target's geometry with a surgical tool's placement is crucial for ensuring the accuracy of medical procedures. Surface-based approaches are often favored for their ease of use and rapid execution, although they encounter significant limitations when dealing with flexible organs, as standard methods typically assume rigid structures. This research introduces an accessible method to align surgical instruments on compliant organs using haptic data. The approach utilizes a lightweight, subject-specific biomechanical model featuring a shell-structure composition: an unstiffened Finite Element Model (FEM) positioned between an input surface defined by data and a response surface generated through mechanical simulation. By migrating the organ's boundary conditions so that the response surface aligns with the actual anatomical structure detected via a sensor, the method captures the structure-buring deformation. Consequently, the initial boundary conditions can be solved iteratively using a strategy such as an upward Gauss-Seidel process. The resulting technique has been validated at the organ level with mechanical testing involving inflated pig bladders, demonstrating a root mean square (RMS) error of 1.8 mm. Subsequent tests using surgical instruments to track a compliant 3D-printed heart phantom yielded less than 0.4 mm RMS error.

The paper investigates the conformal matter-free symmetries specific to the tensor of momentum and energy stored in spheres. By utilizing spherical general relativity, this work categorizes such symmetries into four distinct cases, most being characterized by having three independent generators. Notably, a specific scenario emerges with five independent generators relating to the tensor of momentum and energy stored in spheres and bounded by a single constraint equation for its components.

Self-supervised scene flow estimation relies on minimizing an optimization-based residual, utilizing the optical flow assumptions to generate virtual images. Recent advancements introduced metric learning methods that leverage the smoothness field error directly as a teaching signal, effectively circumventing the flaws of traditional hand-crafted metrics. However, these recent models require an initial "acquaintance" stage running unsupervised flow methods to produce rough flow estimates and extract features; since these predictions are inherently imperfect, the acquired representations remain contaminated with noise. This study investigates these previous 'acquaintance' stages as a vulnerability, demonstrating, through the introduction of a specific adversarial approach, that these rough estimates and embedded features can be exploited adversarially. This attack not only reveals the reliance and dependence of the current method on these preliminary stages but also serves as a broader warning about the trustworthiness of self-generated representations in the context of semi-/self-supervised learning. Consequently, the authors propose a novel framework executing adversarial metric learning exclusively on the unsupervised flow error itself, eliminating the need for an initial acquaintance phase. Experimental results indicate this proposed approach not only secures better robustness against the inherent inconsistencies of self-supervised data but also enhances accuracy relative to the previous state-of-the-art methodology.

In this study, the structure of spin-polarized star-like objects formed by up, down, and strange quarks is examined using the finite-temperature canonical ensemble method applied to both confined and deconfined phases. The thermal equilibrium behavior of these spin-polarized quark stars (SPQS) is analyzed through the Elliott-Jamison equations, incorporating effects of internal and external magnetic fields on the statistical thermodynamics of quarks at finite temperature with full spin polarization. Results indicate that increasing either the internal or external magnetic field reduces both the transition temperature and chemical potential; however, increasing the spin multiplicity has the opposite effect, as does increasing the magnetic field. Specifically, the influence of the external magnetic field intensifies as temperature rises, while this effect weakens as chemical potential increases. At high chemical potential, the transition temperature and its response to variations in external magnetic field diminish. Upward transitions occur only when the product of temperature (in Kelvin) and chemical potential (in eV) exceeds 3351.5$\times$10$^{14}$; otherwise, such transitions are unattainable. Finally, it is suggested that spin-polarized quark matter may exist within the cores of neutron stars.

Kollár's theorem regarding block arrangements asserts that if \(\mathbf{p}\) is a non-constant polynomial with integer coefficients and \( \mathbf{p}(x) \neq 0 \) for all \( x \in \mathbf{Z} \), then there exists an integer \( d > 0 \) such that the set of polynomial values \( \mathbf{S} = \{ \mathbf{p}(x) : \mathbf{x} \in \mathbf{Z} \} \) contains no array of \( d \) consecutive integers, where \( d \) depends only on the field of coefficients of \( \mathbf{p} \) and its degree. This paper presents multiple new instances illustrating this theorem, including the case of the Kollár conjecture confirmed by B. B. Knutson (2023) and several additional families examined here for the first in the literature. We also introduce the notion of strict composition for block arrangements and demonstrate its utility through examples and a characterization of monomials of the form \( x^{k} \) and polynomials with the Chebyshev property within the narrow class of reciprocal irreducible terms. Additionally, we characterize the set of all possible leading coefficients and degrees to build the required array.

This study presents a Partially Grid-Based (PG) approach for the Multiple Birth Filter's (MBF) origin model, where the particle concentration model remains solved exactly using the MBF framework, but the velocity and location components are addressed via a fine grid matching the underlying field. By matching the underlying field's variance, this proposed method—implemented with Binary-Tree-Linked (BTL) structures—significantly reduces computational demands. Each particle in the filter corresponds to a tree in BTL, containing nodes that represent grid cells across BTL. BTL allows for efficient field updates and the collapse of dependent stochastic thinned processes (ST). Initial tests on uniform distributions indicate that this technique outperforms purely grid-dependent approaches, which typically suffer from convergence issues. Subsequent experiments with non-uniform distributions, including those optimized for sensor management, yield the best overall outcomes.

Real-time decision-making in professional soccer depends on the expertise of professional athletes. While soccer players demonstrate high levels of competence, advancing their performance during critical phases of play remains a key objective. This study introduces an advanced decision-support system aimed at suggesting optimal actions in critical soccer situations. First, we categorize game events into four major categories and analyze the contextual factors that define whether a situation is critical. Then, as all events carry strategic importance, we apply Deep Reinforcement Learning to realize state-of-the-art real-time event recommendation capabilities. Finally, specific to critical scenarios, we refine this approach using a Multi-Reference Deep Reinforcement Learning framework, delivering enhanced performance beyond basic recommendations by strategically integrating expert knowledge to upskill the initial model. User feedback indicates that professional soccer agents find these suggestions useful. Consequently, this approach has the potential to generally advance the Deep Reinforcement Learning handling of real-world tasks, while also setting a new standard for integrating prior expertise to facilitate faster convergence in real-world applications.

In data-driven approaches to dialogue prediction, the quality of the model is heavily dependent on the effectiveness of the encoder's information representation. Consequently, understanding these representations is vital; however, current studies often skip over this aspect or focus only over superficial characteristics like variance and confidence intervals. Addressing this gap, this paper analyzes various statistical and semantic properties of the encoders used in common dialogue models. Our investigation utilizes multiple characterizations, including multi-probe tasks, cosine similarity assessments, and auxiliary prediction models. The findings reveal that encoded representations convey more variability and limited predictive power beyond rigorous standard measures.

Ground LiDAR-based place recognition is fundamental to global localization and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) in robotics and autonomous driving systems. Deep learning has enhanced feature extraction for place recognition, with frameworks like PointNet focusing on direct, unlabeled point cloud processing. Nevertheless, existing methods utilizing point-based features often neglect the significance of geometric relations. This study introduces a novel point-to-point attention mechanism within a deep learning framework, forming AttDLNet. By integrating this attention mechanism with convolutional layers, the network efficiently recognizes scenes from 3D LiDAR data. The proposed method was validated using natural and autonomous driving datasets, demonstrating superior performance over current state-of-the-art approaches.

Delivering high-definition streaming services, whether as a part of a broader system or a standalone component, relies heavily on transcoding for compatibility across diverse clients and networks. As cloud infrastructure expands as a primary platform for video preparation, the architectural alignment of applications with available resources becomes critical. To address the performance and efficiency of both cloud allocation strategies and the transcoding process itself, extensive empirical testing was conducted to analyze the impact of various heterogeneous configurations. Complementing these experiments, this study introduces corresponding mathematical models that reflect the observed performance based on these diverse settings. Ultimately, the research reveals two key insights: (1) Heterogeneous environments require careful application design and modeling to optimize performance, and (2), the assumption that virtual machine (VM) synchronization does not impede processing must be replaced with proactive, predictive models.

Accurately predicting river flow velocities and water depths is vital for various sectors, including weather and climate science, ecological management, and disaster preparedness. Traditional computational methods for modeling these shallow water flows are often constrained by slow simulation speeds. This study introduces a fast-learning deep regression model designed to provide an instant and precise alternative for predicting shallow water flow velocity and depth. The model was trained on a broad spectrum of randomly generated and physically consistent initial conditions for the shallow water equations, utilizing an efficient dataset creation strategy. By leveraging the Chamfer distance metric, the model received supervision to ensure outputs aligned with results from a traditional numerical solver, focusing specifically on mass and momentum conservation. When evaluated on the same training data, the model demonstrated virtually error-free accuracy; however, despite being trained exclusively on a single dataset, its ability to generalize to unseen data is strong even across diverse distributions. The resulting regression model achieves convergence within approximately 10 milliseconds on a standard CPU, providing input-independent simulation results in such a brief timeframe. While initial conditions in the training data were not physically valid, the model's ability to converge to accurate, physically valid results indicates successful regularization and a capacity for significant generalization.

Metacoustic materials, which feature periodic variations in density and elastic properties, enable the manipulation of mechanical wave propagation, often resulting in effects like phononic bandgap formation and unusual thermal conduction. Acoustic metagratings, a specific subtype, utilize periodic discontinuities to induce topological transformations (Bogoliubov-Umbreho transformations) and induce momentum changes exceeding a single lattice vector. While recent advancements have explored natural media for natural wave propagation, engineering artificial surfaces remains a potent strategy for achieving material-specific wave behaviors. However, previous efforts to fabricate such acoustic metagratings are constrained by traditional methods, which struggle with micro-features necessary for ultrahigh frequencies, often resulting in significant energy loss. To overcome existing manufacturing limitations, we present the first acoustic metagrating fabricated at a microliter scale using two-photon lithography. Experimental results confirm the device's functionality up to 25 kHz and demonstrate effective sound redirection at lower frequencies, specifically around 7.5 kHz. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical framework predicting both the performance and radiated sound field at these ultra-micro scales, establishing a crucial foundation for future acoustic metamaterial research aimed at unnatural momentum transfer.

Gels and vitrimers are defects-free, continuous networks that exhibit strength and toughness comparable to solids, while maintaining the elasticity and capacity for large, reversible deformations found in elastomers. Recent discoveries have revealed that these robust, defect-free gels can be replaced by distinct assemblies known as "rafts." Rafts consist of entangled polymer chains arranged in tight loops tied with narrow gaps no wider than a few nanometers. Although these gaps are too small to let macromolecules escape, they effectively stop the propagation of mechanical failures. Consequently, rafts combine high elastic modulus and strong ultimate stress with exceptional capacity for dissipated energy. This work reviews the design, properties, and functional applications of narrow gaps in polymer networks and addresses the molecular behaviors of flexible chains near narrow constrictions, including how these factors guide the optimization of performance in such systems and their potential use as reliable, reusable mechanical components with integrated self-healing capabilities.

This study introduces a directional emissions index, defined as the exponential negative entropy of the far-field distribution, to characterize the directionality of laser beams. Within statistical mechanics, entropy characterizes the likelihood of a system's state; in directional emission measurements, it quantifies divergence. While mean divergence is typically used for Gaussian beams, high-quality (non-Gaussian) lasers—arising from optical resonators or micro-resonators launched by single-mode cavity modes—require such an index. Because high-directionality beams possess sharp peaks and narrow divergence, their full-fractional moments are heavily influenced by fluctuational noise in the far-field. Consequently, high-directionity evaluations should focus on a limited set of moments near the amplitude peak. To achieve this, the proposed index utilizes only negative entropy formed from an inverted (flipped and shifted) normalized far-field profile. This approach eliminates normalization errors and delivers a quantitative diversity-free index. The method was validated using High-Q VCSELs and GaAs/Al macro-mirror devices, demonstrating sensitivity to changes in vertical directionality.

We examine how a laser traps a thermal atomic cloud and investigate how this confinement alters the correlation between far-field intensity fluctuations at frequency components separated by a Doppler shift. Furthermore, we introduce an intuitive model showing how to maximize non-gaussian light statistics—specifically squizzed or super-rough intensity fluctuations—by adjusting the trapping geometry.

Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) involves learning from a stored dataset, where the dataset itself is defined as following an underlying multi-agent policy. In traditional MARL approaches, this multi-agent policy is treated as a black box. However, in practical applications, datasets often implicitly contain additional information beyond what the original policy generated—for example, good paths followed by agents that were not necessarily taking random actions but exploring effective strategies. This paper introduces a novel offline MARL framework wherein certain good paths attributed to agents not fully captured by their respective policies are incorporated. By applying standard offline MARL methods to good paths while using regular dataset samples to constrain the model, we prevent overfitting on repeated actions found in standard data. To operationalize this, the authors define a specific metric to identify these good paths and utilize it as a dual-objective function. The resulting algorithm, termed OGMPO (Offline Good Multi-agent Path Offsets for Multi-agent Optimization), aims to traverse trajectories more efficiently by prioritizing these good paths. Experimental validation on both municipal driving and MuJoCo benchmarks confirms that OGMPO outperforms existing state-of-the-art offline MARL techniques.

The accelerating pace of scientific discovery poses significant challenges to both fundamental research and applied problem-solving, prompting intense scrutiny on factors that boost scientific output. While education and research spending are widely recognized as legitimate drivers, the contentious nature of measuring "productivity"—often measured merely by publication counts—has emerged as a critical issue. This study conducts a preliminary analysis based on a representative dataset: abstracts describing the research endeavors of all authors listed in the "Computer Society Conference Publications" corpus, which we believe provides a solid foundation for further exploration. Our analysis reveals a pronounced divergence between measured productivity and the actual volume of knowledge, and we question the suitability of using such metrics to evaluate the careers of individual researchers or to evaluate the health of the broader scientific enterprise.

This paper addresses physical layer security (PLS) in dual-agent wireless systems consisting of two users transmitting multicarrier data via an amplify-and-forward (AF) relay under jamming attacks. To maximize the secrecy wire rate (SWR), a joint optimization problem is formulated, coordinating power allocation for information and jamming signals. Recognizing that this problem is non-convex, the proposed solution introduces a diagonal precoder, transforming the task into a series of subproblems. These subproblems allow the approach to first determine the optimal operating carrier and develop convenient formulas for calculating jamming power. Subsequently, an alternative optimization technique is applied to derive the optimal allocation of transmitting and jamming power. Simulation outcomes validate the efficacy of the proposed methodology.

We examine a model in which a non-trivial topological structure interacts with an electromagnetic field through the tight-binding framework, focusing specifically on the topology of multi-mode quantum electro-dynamics. Our analysis reveals that placing a dipole defect along the topological structure leads to anomalous decay dynamics and alters the spectrum of the intrinsic vacuum state compared to single-mode QED scenarios. Furthermore, by positioning a local defect within a topological arrangement that supports Dirac points—rather than a traditional linear guide—we demonstrate the creation of trapped states residing exclusively in the defect location. Last, but not least, our findings indicate enhanced effective coupling between individual particles and photons when the system operates within the topological configuration.

Automated vehicles (AVs) operating in mixed autonomous and human-driven environments face significant prediction and control challenges. Specifically anticipating the maneuvers of stochastic human drivers while maintaining robustness against modeling inaccuracies and sensory noise is particularly difficult. This paper introduces two interconnected modules designed for an AV navigating a traffic-lighted intersection: a neighborhood-based human driver behavior prediction model and a safety-aware predictive controller. The prediction model leverages short-term, data-driven simulations to assess potential future actions before generating current driving observations, thereby combining the flexibility of predictive learning with the reliability of supervised methods to enhance prediction accuracy. The accompanying controller integrates this model with Model Predictive Control to optimize speed commands; it targets potential collisions with peers by deriving set-invariance signals from the predicted behavior data, ensuring signal compliance, minimal stopping frequencies, and smooth progression. Using extensive high-fidelity numerical simulations featuring diverse driving configurations, the study validates the proposed framework's efficacy in mitigating collisions among automated vehicles, reducing emission levels, promoting smooth driving, and maintaining shorter waiting times for both AVs and their human-driven counterparts.

Text-based games provide an excellent framework for evaluating language understanding, complex problem-solving, and common-sense reasoning in AI systems. This paper introduces a novel formulation for generating numerically accurate equilibrium configurations of rotating stars within the framework of general relativity. Utilizing a Lagrangian formulation of the Einstein field equations and the Euler equation, we derive a conserved vector field that leads to a set of coupled partial differential equations. These equations dictate the star's structure, with solutions specifying the temporal and spatial components of the corotating four-velocity, as well as the specific enthalpy. Due to the partial differential nature of this system, it necessitates solution via finite element methods. To validate this approach, we apply it to compute the solutions first proposed by Hinderer et al. (2009) in their numerical study of rapidly rotating stars. Our results for mass, angular momentum, and radius show excellent agreement with those of Hinderer, while detailed comparisons of our internal structure calculations with their findings confirm the reliability of this new formulation. Building on this validated foundation, we develop an algorithm to generate a sequence of adiabatically evolving, rotating stellar states. Unlike previous integration methods constrained to a Cartesian grid and facing memory limitations, our method is step-size independent, memory efficient, and avoids the need for re-configuring the solution algorithm. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating angular momentum as a fixed parameter is superior to using angular speed for this iterative process. Finally, we utilize this evolution algorithm to investigate the response of both non-motivated and primordially rotating stars to a sudden tidal disturbance.

Achieving high-precision automatic extraction for complex, multi-step paper layouts remains a significant challenge, particularly given the need to invest heavily in developing accurate models. A key strategy to lower the cost of labeling is the use of self-supervised pre-training, yet a bottleneck persists: producing large volumes of self-supervised "pseudo-gold" data requires substantial human effort. To overcome this, we introduce "SuperAnnotations," a human-centric data-formatting approach where annotators handle entire classes of documents at once using formatting tools to generate pseudo-gold data efficiently. We demonstrate that SuperAnnotations enable the collection of 100 million formatted data-point equivalents per hour—yielding 10 times more self-supervised training data per hour than standard methods. Additionally, experimental results show that utilizing this self-supplied data alongside well-trained transformers, rather than simple identity mappings, can enhance data-labeling efficiency by a factor of 10. A crucial takeaway is that while self-supervised techniques excel at reducing costs for model initialization, they must be paired with properly formatted pseudo-gold strings to further boost performance above the baseline.

The number of observations available for gravitational waves (GWs) from binary compact object (CO) mergers is gradually increasing, as detectors within existing installations continue to improve and newer platforms with greater sensitivity and bandwidth are prepared for future use. Neutron star-Black Hole (NSBH) COs represent one of the primary potential sources within the GW detection landscape, leading to ongoing advancements in both traditional modeling methods and machine learning (ML) applications. This study introduces an enhanced version of Fully Connected Neural Networks (FCNN), incorporating over-complete and encoder components, to achieve faster convergence and higher precision in analyzing GWs originating from NSBH mergers. By training on subsets of the Surtio GW database containing NLBH sources, the model demonstrates a significant 10-fold acceleration in inference speed using CPU resources compared to standard fully connected architectures, alongside a 500-fold improvement over generic ML classification pipelines, all while maintaining accurate source identification capabilities. Furthermore, when compared to the number of online, fully connected binaries for inference using a similar training set size (150,000), the proposed component required a substantially smaller training data volume to reach equivalent performance metrics, effectively cutting down data collection times from an estimated ~4 months (based on collecting 150,000 GWs) to just 1 week (gathering 2,000 GWs).

This work evaluates the security of numerical overlay multiple access (NOMA) protocols by analyzing an scenario where a hacker attempts to decode sufficient information to gain access. We introduce a novel security metric, named decoded rate (DR), which quantifies the number of commands the adversary successfully interprets. Assuming the opponent utilizes the optimal strategy to maximize this decoded rate, we formulate it as an investment problem aimed at determining the most effective attack approach. Solving the associated dynamic programming equations allows us to determine the approximate value function, enabling an approximate resolution to the discrete time borrowing problem. Comparisons between the derived solution and heuristic attacks highlight notable disparities in performance. Finally, we examine the impact of various initial conditions on both the DR and the value function.

In response to the high computational costs of Finite Element Method (FEM) solutions for Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) problems, Reduced Basis Methods (RBMM) have been introduced to mitigate this burden. Current methods for representing and navigating unknown 2D environments typically rely on complete binary maps, generated by OR'ing individual occupancy columns. While effective, this approach consumes excessive memory and causes prolonged loading times, thereby hindering real-world applications. To mitigate these inefficiencies without increasing error rates, we introduce **HiTMap**, a compact yet precise hierarchical topological map representation. The project's objectives involved developing a mapping algorithm capable of converting point clouds into HiTMap and creating a corresponding navigation system. We validated our solutions through both laboratory tests and real-world deployments across three distinct scenarios. The study revealed that across all environments, both the binary maps and HiTMap achieved identical labeling accuracy. Furthermore, tests demonstrated that HiTMap consumes significantly less memory and facilitates substantially faster data loading.

Precise magnetic field measurements at high sensitivity are crucial for multiple high-tech applications, such as those involving quantum sensors and superconducting qubits. This paper demonstrates that measuring local magnetic field fluctuations can be executed with exceptional sensitivity via atomic interferometry facilitated by the Meissner effect in a superconductor, functioning as both a reflective surface and a device inducing a phase shift. When a non-magnetic atom approaches a superconductor, quantum mechanics dictates it enters a quantum Hall state, creating a wave-like superflow that creates a magnetic potential barrier known as the "magnetic wall." As an atom gets closer to the surface, it reflects off this wall, generating a wave whose length is determined by how close the atom is to the superconductor. As the atom moves toward the "magnetic wall," its wave function acquires a phase change, making atomic reflection sensitive to minuscule variations in the atom's distance from a superconductor, allowing an atom bouncer to detect very small changes in a atom's wave function due to its position. Because the effect of a atom bouncer on an atom's wave function is due to its position, any variations in the atom's distance can cause large phase changes, which allows an atom interferometer to detect variations in a atom's wave function at a superconductor. As a result, atomic variations in a atom bouncer allow for precise measurements to be made on atomic distances, making it possible to detect changes in a atom's wave function

The magnetothermal effect (MTE) manifests as a generation of transverse voltage in magnetically polarized materials exposed to a temperature gradient. Recently, research has concentrated on developing room-temperature MTE within magnetic transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs). This study explores the magnetothermal properties of magnetically polarized spin-split edge states in heterostructured armchair-hexagonal TMD moiré superlattices, utilizing a semi- classical transport framework. We demonstrate that a magnetothermal field perpendicular to the initial magnetic field can produce voltage signal components in both primary directions: signal component in primary direction; additionally, a thermal field along the initial magnetic field enhances signal magnitude. Findi indicate a strong magnetic sensitivity for this direction; furthermore, signal direction changes from signal to opposite based on configuration. These findings identify a previously unexplored MTE mechanism in magnetic TMDs: proximity-induced long-range MTE across edge states, which may offer a novel strategy to detect and manipulate spins and magnetism in twisted TMD systems.

We investigate how light propagates across a planar vacuum-metal interface with minimal to zero gap distances, examining the transitions from both classical and quantum spill-out models alongside a nonlocal hydrodynamic approach. While conventional classical theories predict that longitudinal (gap-plasmon) modes retain high confinement and frequency as the gap disappears—causing divergence and aggregation of charges at the interface leading to divergence and charge densities that explode near the interface—these findings reveal distinct behaviors for spill-out and nonlocality which maintain constant frequency and coordinates along the interface but keep linear charges densities finite. Experimental data supports the latter, indicating that quantum effects dominate in ultra-narrow gaps exceeding 0.5 nm, a range where non-local charges densities finite. These observations provide important guidelines for engineering devices involving sub-nanometer gaps.
